prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, opening a new regime of precision in the measurement of time and frequency

statement.case_for: B012 is the only shortlisted candidate that is simultaneously a clean invention, an experimentally decisive demonstration, a field-opening measurement capability and a result that several independent laboratories have reproduced. The magic-wavelength idea lets one interrogate very many atoms with Doppler and recoil effects suppressed, and the experiments then delivered fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, resolution of the gravitational redshift over millimetre height differences, and clock-to-clock comparisons over fibre. Those are numbers that can be checked in a lab book, not rhetoric. It also has consequences beyond the clock itself: a redefinition of the second is on the agenda, and the clocks are used in searches for varying constants and dark matter and in relativistic geodesy. Seven of eight members ranked it, and the two-name attribution (Katori for the concept and early Sr work, Ye for driving accuracy, stability and many-body clock physics) is unusually clean for a modern experimental prize. The 2005 prize covered the frequency comb, and the 2012 prize covered ion control, but neither covered the neutral-atom lattice scheme, so this is a distinct advance.
statement.case_against: My own first place is the one most exposed to the charge of being a specialist's choice, since five colleagues put it at rank 5 and the subject is narrow in its direct audience. Priority is not entirely tidy: Ye's group and Katori's group, as well as ion-clock groups (Al+ and Yb+ clocks reach comparable accuracy) and Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and others in the lattice-clock lineage, all contributed, and a committee could reasonably ask whether the prize should be broader, for example including an ion clock or the stabilized-laser work that limits stability. The strongest practical payoff, the redefinition of the second and clock-based geodesy, is still to come, so one can argue the impact is promised rather than delivered. Finally, the 2005 prize partly occupies the precision-frequency territory.

responses.point: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice and Ye's strontium realization are a quantitative, understood route to 1e-18 precision with several independent labs, and two names are a fair configuration; she also ranks atom interferometry B003 second.
responses.response: I agree on the attribution and on maturity, and I appreciate the point that the 2005 comb prize does not cover this. Where I would qualify your view is on B003: I ranked it second myself, but as an experimentalist I see a real difference in what has been delivered. Lattice clocks have reached their headline accuracy and are being compared across continents, whereas atom interferometry's headline goals (equivalence-principle tests at the 1e-15 level, gravitational-wave detection) are still being pursued, and the credit there is shared with Chu, who has already been honoured. I would therefore keep B003 as a strong alternative but not as a co-recipient in a two-part prize at this time.

responses.point: B029, the IceCube discovery of astrophysical neutrinos, opens a new observational window through decades of calibration and systematics control; Pearce ranks it first and B012 second.
responses.response: I take the instrument-driven argument seriously, and it is the kind of work I respect. The diffuse flux is robust and was a real discovery. My reservation is attribution rather than science: IceCube is a collaboration of several hundred people built on the Baikal and AMANDA predecessors, and the credited trio (Halzen, Karle, Spiering) cannot be defended as obviously the right three without more evidence on who made the decisive analysis and construction contributions. B012 has no such problem, and I would be happy to see B029 as the other part of a two-part prize if the committee can settle the names, but I would not put it ahead of B012 while that question is open.

responses.point: B036, magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene, is a theory-predicted flat-band condition confirmed by experiment that opened correlated insulators and superconductivity and was independently reproduced by many groups; he ranks it first.
responses.response: The prediction-then-measurement story is attractive and the reproduction across groups is impressive. As a measurement-oriented member, my questions are about stability of the interpretation: mehlig-bernhard notes that the origin of the superconductivity is still debated and the sample-dependence (twist-angle disorder) is notorious. I also doubt that the theory share should be split across MacDonald and Bistritzer while Jarillo-Herrero takes the experiment, since that makes the prize rely on a one-experiment discovery from 2018. I do not say the work is unworthy; I say the field is younger and less settled than lattice clocks, and the clock community is already preparing a redefinition of the second.

responses.point: B057, the Z2 topological insulator and quantum spin Hall effect, is a universal mechanism with a bulk invariant fixing edge transport, a theory-plus-experiment pairing; he ranks it first but acknowledges the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission and the 2016 prize overlap.
responses.response: I agree that the Kane-Mele and Molenkamp pairing is conceptually elegant, and I would not dispute the field's scale. But you yourself identify the real gap: the HgTe prediction by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is not in the credited trio, and the 2016 prize already honoured topological phases. I cannot weigh the conceptual originality as strongly as you do, because from my side what I want is experimental evidence that the field has opened measurement possibilities; the quantized edge conductance is a very small number of experiments by a small number of groups. If the committee wants a condensed-matter part, I would rather see that allocation problem solved than glossed over.

responses.point: B051, circuit QED, is a clean discovery-plus-platform case with a coherent Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf trio, and it underlies most superconducting processors; he ranks it first.
responses.response: I ranked it sixth, and the reason is not scientific quality. Circuit QED is excellent physics and the trio is coherent. I place it lower because the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits has just recognised closely related ground, and because the claim of impact rests heavily on quantum computers whose usefulness is not demonstrated yet. I do think that is a fair difference of weighting, not a disagreement about the science. Your point that it has been reproduced in Yale, ETH, Delft and Chalmers is a strong one, and I would move it up if it could be shown that its discoveries, as opposed to its engineering, are what the citation would honour.

uncertainties: Whether the committee wants to honour precision-frequency metrology again so soon after 2005 and 2012, or prefers a different area.
Whether a prize for lattice clocks should also credit the ion-clock lineage or the ultrastable-laser work behind clock stability; the supplied credit leaves both out.
The relative priority of Katori's and Ye's contributions to the early strontium demonstrations, which I have taken from memory rather than from the documents.
Whether a second part (B003, B029 or B028) would strengthen or dilute the configuration, since each has its own attribution problem.
statement.conflict_note: I spent time in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder during my PhD, and Hall is Jun Ye's doctoral advisor and a JILA colleague; I have no joint work or financial interest with Katori or Ye, but the committee should note this lineage connection. I am also a rare-earth-crystal and slow-light person, not a clock person, and I have no connection to the other shortlisted candidates, though my WACQT role overlaps institutionally with Chalmers, where Göran Johansson works and which is relevant to B051.
